text.headline: Knoxville Coffee Crawl
text.text:
Research question: How did Knoxville’s coffee culture grow from an industrial roasting town into a city of independent coffee shops, and why have those shops become important gathering places in Knoxville today?

Ratings are from Google Maps as of November 2026. Read a text-only version of this tour.

text.headline: History: JFG Coffee
text.text:
Historic stop · 1926–2000s

Address: 200 W. Jackson Ave. (now JFG Flats)

Long before lattes, Knoxville made coffee by the factory load. JFG, named for founder James Franklin Goodson’s initials, moved its roasting to Jackson Avenue in 1926. In the mid-1930s it moved into a former hat factory nearby, which is now the JFG Flats apartments. Historian Jack Neely writes that “for 80 years, the northern part of downtown Knoxville smelled like roasting coffee.”

Reily Foods bought the company in 1965, but the restored JFG sign near the Gay Street Bridge is still a landmark. In this era, coffee in Knoxville was mostly an industry. The idea of the coffee shop as a place to gather came later.

Sources: Neely, “A Caffeinated History of Coffee & Tea in Knoxville” (Visit Knoxville, 2025); Know Your Knox: the JFG sign

text.headline: History: Old City Java
text.text:
Historic stop · opened 1990

Address: 109 S. Central St.

When Old City Java opened in 1990, “several years before Starbucks got here,” Neely writes that it “struck some people as a strange fad.” In the 1960s, most Knoxvillians had been drinking instant coffee or Sanka.

The fad lasted: Old City Java may now be the oldest business still operating in the Old City. It marks a turning point in this story, when coffee became a reason to sit down and stay. Sociologists call a spot like this a “third place,” somewhere to belong besides home and work.

Sources: Neely, “A Caffeinated History of Coffee & Tea in Knoxville” (Visit Knoxville, 2025)

text.headline: Capybara Coffee
text.text:
Tucked into University Commons, Capybara Coffee is about a five-minute walk from campus. Sadly, there are no real capybaras, but the vibes are adorable and the coffee is excellent.

Capybara centers Brazilian coffee culture, with beans from Casa Brasil and teas from Smith Teamaker. It has also teamed up with UT’s Plant Sciences Club on a student plant-adoption event. Being close to campus helps, but events and a clear personality are what make it a gathering place as well as a coffee stop.

Address: 2457 University Commons Way
Rating: 4.8/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Sources: Visit Knoxville: Knoxville’s Coffee Scene; UT calendar: Plant Adoption with Capybara Coffee

text.headline: New Here Coffee
text.text:
Right beneath The Hub apartments on the Strip, New Here is just a street away from campus and one of the best study spots in town.

New Here sits beneath student housing on one of the busiest streets near campus. Its location shows one way coffee shops fit into student life: a place to study or meet friends, right below where people live.

Address: 1915 Cumberland Ave.
Rating: 4.2/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

text.headline: Coffee 360
text.text:
In the heart of Fort Sanders, Coffee 360 serves a wide variety of flavors and baked goods, a convenient stop for students who live off campus. It also partners with local apartment complexes on monthly “Bagel Socials.”

The Bagel Socials show how a coffee shop can build community beyond its own walls, giving neighbors in different apartment buildings a reason to meet.

Address: 111 S. 17th St.
Rating: 4.7/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

text.headline: Jacks
text.text:
On Gay Street at the edge of the Old City, Jacks has a vibe unlike any other coffee shop in the area. Along with coffee, it sells plants and other fun goods, and it has a second location on North Central Street.

Katherine and Logan Higgins opened Jacks in February 2019 as a shop for local makers, starting with 17 Knoxville vendors. Coffee and plants came later, through partners Mark and Kendell Lily, and the North Central Street shop followed in 2021. Jacks shows how a coffee shop can also support a local economy.

Address: 133 S. Gay St.
Rating: 4.4/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Sources: Inside of Knoxville: Jacks Opens Today (2019); Inside of Knoxville: Jacks’ Second Location (2021)

text.headline: Treetop Coffee Shop
text.text:
Treetop’s second shop opened on Gay Street in September 2026, inside the new Lone Tree Pass development.

Treetop began as a coffee truck run by best friends Courtney Dooley and Rachel Casstevens. Their Sequoyah Hills shop followed in 2021 and is still open. The downtown shop is part of a $30 million development with condos and restaurants, and one article described the plan as “a new gathering spot in the heart of downtown.” Treetop’s growth also raises a question: as downtown adds new condos, who are its gathering places for?

Address: 255 S. Gay St. (Lone Tree Pass)
Rating: 5/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026; newly opened)

Sources: Hayes, “3 additions to Knoxville’s caffeine scene” (Knox News via Yahoo, 2026); What Now: Treetop Coffee at Lone Tree Pass (2026)

text.headline: K Brew Downtown
text.text:
K Brew’s downtown shop is on Gay Street, just off the lobby of the Embassy Suites hotel.

Brothers Pierce and Michael LaMacchia founded K Brew in 2013, and Pierce is a UT alumnus. The downtown shop opened with the hotel in November 2019, with bar seats facing Gay Street and more seating throughout the lobby. A local shop inside a national hotel puts visitors and Knoxvillians in the same room, and makes an unlikely spot feel like Knoxville.

Address: 507 S. Gay St. (Embassy Suites)
Rating: 4.6/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Sources: Inside of Knoxville: K Brew Downtown Opens on Gay Street (2019); Visit Knoxville: Knoxville’s Coffee Scene; UT CCI: Pierce LaMacchia (2024)

text.headline: Honeybee Coffee Co.
text.text:
Take a short trip across the river into South Knoxville and you’ll find Honeybee Coffee Co., one of the best coffee shops outside of downtown. On top of great coffee, it has views of the river and a large lounge to enjoy your latte in. Hours have changed recently, so check before you go.

Honeybee started in 2014 as an Airstream coffee trailer downtown and opened here in January 2017. The building dates to about 1924, and from 1939 it housed Charlie’s Cafe, which served workers from a nearby meatpacking plant and bus shop. People have been gathering here for generations.

Its story also shows how fragile these places can be. In 2024, a failed ownership sale and a staff walkout closed most Honeybee locations, and as of that July only this shop remained open.

Address: 700 Sevier Ave.
Rating: 4.5/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Sources: Knox Mercury: The Slow Rebirth of Sevier Avenue (2017); Knox News: Honeybee’s 10-year history (2024)

text.headline: Awaken Coffee at Kern’s
text.text:
Awaken Coffee at Kern’s serves ethically sourced coffee and handcrafted drinks inside Kern’s Food Hall in South Knoxville.

Awaken began in the Old City, where Adam and Sarah Lutts opened their first shop at 125 W. Jackson Avenue in January 2016. They wanted to be more connected to downtown, and planned to use the back room as a meeting place for their church. From the start, the shop was meant to bring people together.

The Kern’s building adds another layer. The Kern company moved to its Chapman Highway plant in 1931, and bread was made there for decades. Like JFG’s old factory, it has gone from making food and drink for the city to a new life, this time as a place to gather.

Address: 2201 Kern’s Rising Way (Kern’s Food Hall)
Rating: 4.7/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Sources: Kern’s Bakery: Awaken Coffee; Inside of Knoxville: Awaken Coffee Opens in the Old City (2016); Wikipedia: Peter Kern

text.headline: Conclusion: Why These Shops Matter
text.text:
Knoxville’s coffee story begins with an industry. JFG made coffee something the city produced, and the smell of roasting filled the northern part of downtown. With Old City Java in 1990, coffee became something to share in person.

Today’s shops matter because each gives a community somewhere to be. Capybara and New Here serve students, Coffee 360 brings apartment neighbors together, Jacks supports local makers, and Treetop and K Brew bring Knoxville businesses to a changing Gay Street. Honeybee carries a working-class building into a reviving neighborhood, and Awaken helps turn an old bread factory into a gathering place.

These places can be fragile, as Honeybee’s troubles in 2024 show, and they may not feel welcoming or affordable to everyone. Still, they help show how Knoxville went from a town that roasted coffee to a city that gathers around it.

text.text:
Tool: StoryMapJS (Knight Lab), hosted on GitHub Pages; base map © OpenStreetMap contributors.

Method: Present-day shops were chosen by Google Maps rating near UT and downtown (November 2026). Add your site visits and interviews here.

Accessibility: A text-only version of every stop works with screen readers and keyboards. Images include alt text and captions.
